summary: This document defines a portion of the SNMP Management Information Base. It describes objects used for monitoring the Resource Public Key Infrastructure (RPKI) to Router protocol.

eli5.summary: This gives network tools a standard set of dials to watch how routers get their trusted route information.

questions: what is the rpki router mib
how to monitor rpki cache servers with snmp
subtitle: An SNMP MIB module for watching a router's connections to RPKI cache servers.

tldr.problem: Routers that get validated route-origin data from RPKI cache servers over the RPKI-Router Protocol give operators no standard way to monitor those connections over SNMP.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines the RPKI-ROUTER-MIB module with a cache server table, an errors table, a prefix origin table and two notifications, all read-only.
tldr.outcome: A management station can see connection state, message counters, error counts and the prefix and origin AS data a router has received. The module is registered as { mib-2 218 }.

today: RFC 6945 is a Proposed Standard from May 2013, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It monitors the protocol of RFC 6810.

sections.title: Introduction and Framework
sections.content: This RFC defines a portion of the Management Information Base (MIB) used to monitor the RPKI-Router Protocol of RFC 6810. The RFC uses the Internet-Standard Management Framework: managed objects live in a virtual information store called the MIB, usually accessed with the Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP), and defined with the Structure of Management Information (SMI). The module is written in SMIv2 (RFC 2578, RFC 2579 and RFC 2580).
sections.eli5: A MIB is a menu of things a network tool can ask a device about. This RFC adds a new section to the menu for routers that use RPKI.

sections.title: Overview of the Module
sections.content:
The module is split into three tables. The RPKI-Router Cache Server (Connection) Table holds the state and current activity of each connection to an RPKI cache server, plus counters for messages received and sent and for announcements, withdrawals and active records. The Cache Server Errors Table holds counters of errors seen on those connections. The Prefix Origin Table holds IP prefixes with their minimum and maximum prefix lengths and the origin Autonomous System (AS), collected from all the cache servers the router is connected to.

Two notifications tell a Network Management Station (NMS) or operator about changes in connection state. The module sits under the object identifier { mib-2 218 }, which IANA assigned, and all its objects are read-only.
sections.eli5: There are three notebooks: one about each helper connection, one about mistakes, and one listing which network is allowed to announce which addresses.

sections.title: The Cache Server Table
sections.content:
Each row describes one connection to a cache server and is indexed by the remote address type, remote address and remote port. Other columns give the local address and port, the router's preference for the server (lower is more preferred; the maximum Unsigned32 value is returned if no order is configured), the connection type, and a status of up(1) or down(2).

The connection type is one of ssh(1), tls(2), tcpMD5(3), tcpAO(4), tcp(5), ipsec(6) or other(7). Counters cover messages received and sent, and IPv4 and IPv6 announcements and withdrawals, while gauges give the active IPv4 and IPv6 record counts. Further objects hold the latest serial number, the session ID (0 to 65535), the configured refresh timer (60 to 7200 seconds) and the seconds left until the next refresh. A negative time-to-refresh means the refresh is overdue by that many seconds.

Every row has a unique rpkiRtrCacheServerId, which is the key used to find the prefix origin rows created from that connection. A scalar, rpkiRtrDiscontinuityTimer, gives the sysUpTime at which any Counter32 object in the module last had a discontinuity, so that managers only compare values received since then.

If the remote address exceeds 114 octets, the index values exceed the 128 sub-identifier limit and the row cannot be accessed over SNMPv1, SNMPv2c or SNMPv3.
sections.eli5: For each helper the router talks to, there is a page showing whether the line is up, how many messages went back and forth, and when the next check is due.

sections.title: Errors and Prefix Origins
sections.content:
The errors table extends each cache server row with eight counters, useful for debugging: Corrupt Data, Internal Error, No Data Available, Invalid Request, Unsupported Protocol Version, Unsupported PDU Type, Withdrawal of Unknown Record and Duplicate Announcement Received. Each counts errors received from the cache server at the other end.

The prefix origin table lists prefixes announced to this router by cache servers. Each row is indexed by address type, address, minimum length, maximum length, the origin AS number and the cache server ID. The AS number is the one authorized to announce the prefix or sub-prefixes it covers, and the maximum length must be greater than or equal to the minimum. If a cache server is removed from the local configuration, its rows are removed from this table.
sections.eli5: One notebook tallies the kinds of mistakes the helper reports. Another lists which network owner is allowed to announce which addresses, and which helper said so.

sections.title: Notifications and Compliance
sections.content:
Two notifications exist. rpkiRtrCacheServerConnectionStateChange signals a change in a connection's status. rpkiRtrCacheServerConnectionToGoStale signals that a connection is about to go stale, and it is suggested to send it when the time-to-refresh drops below 60 seconds. The agent MUST throttle each so that there is at least a 5 second gap between them. For the state-change notification, if several occurred in that window only the most recent is sent at the end of the gap.

The compliance statement is named rpkiRtrRFC6945ReadOnlyCompliance. The cache server, prefix origin and notifications groups are mandatory, and the errors group is optional. An implementation must support the IPv4, IPv6 and DNS address types for the cache server addresses, and IPv4 and IPv6 for prefix origins.
sections.eli5: The router can ring a bell when a line goes up or down, or when a check is almost overdue, but it will not ring more often than once every five seconds.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The module defines no writable objects, so if it is implemented correctly an intruder cannot alter or create its objects through SNMP SET. Readable objects may still be sensitive, since seeing them could help an attacker plan an attack on the router or cache server, so GET and NOTIFY access should be controlled and values possibly encrypted in transit.

Implementations MUST provide the SNMPv3 security features, including authentication and privacy via the User-based Security Model with AES (RFC 3414, RFC 3826). They MAY also support the Transport Security Model with a secure transport such as SSH or TLS/DTLS. Deploying SNMP versions before SNMPv3 is NOT RECOMMENDED.
sections.eli5: Nobody can change these gauges, but peeking at them could still help a troublemaker, so only the right people should be allowed to look.
